title: Negative Power Prices Sweep Europe — But the Gas-Carbon Dynamic Is Shifting
hook: Day-ahead power hit €6.85/MWh in the UK, €7.61/MWh in Nordics. EU carbon at €75.18. The solar spring surge is crushing spark spreads, but coal-to-gas switching still supports gas demand at the margin.
authorWord: Negative power prices are a gas bear signal in the short term — they suppress gas-for-power demand. But carbon at €75+ keeps coal uneconomic for anything but peaking. The real gas-for-power story is winter 2026/27, not today's solar glut.
author: Henry 🦉
details:
European day-ahead power prices have collapsed to multi-month lows. British, Nordic and Dutch markets registered their lowest daily averages since October 2025 at €6.85, €7.61 and €14.46/MWh respectively in early May, per Euronews. Negative power prices have occurred across several bidding zones, driven by abundant solar generation and weak demand. The Euronews analysis highlights this "isn't a good thing" — it signals market distortions that may deter future investment in flexible generation capacity.

EU carbon permits (EUA) at €75.18 (close 08 May), ▲+0.07% on the day, ▲+1.98% MoM, ▲+6.80% YoY, per Trading Economics / ICE. Carbon has been quietly strengthening through the spring, supported by: (1) EU ETS market stability reserve (MSR) continuing to withdraw allowances, (2) front-loading of compliance buying ahead of the annual surrender deadline, and (3) reduced free allocation to heavy industry under the EU's Fit for 55 program. The EUA Dec '26 contract trades near €73.04, per Investing.com data, showing a modest backwardation — the market expects prices to ease slightly from current levels.

Clean dark spread and clean spark spread implications: At EUA €75, the clean dark spread (coal generation margin) remains negative or near-zero for most European coal plants, especially in Germany and the Netherlands. This means coal-to-gas switching remains economically viable at the margin, supporting gas demand for baseload generation. However, with power prices at €6-15/MWh in many zones, even gas generation margins (clean spark spread) are squeezed. The net effect: gas is the marginal fuel but is being priced out by renewables during peak solar hours.

Nordic hydro constraints support continental power prices indirectly. With Norway's hydro deficit persisting (see Weather & Demand card), Nordic power exports to Germany and the UK remain reduced. This normally would support continental power prices, but the solar spring surge is overwhelming this effect. As we move into summer, solar generation will peak, keeping pressure on daytime power prices. Evening and nighttime prices (when solar drops off) will see wider spreads.

Household electricity prices: EU average remains elevated. Eurostat data shows household prices at €38.69/100kWh in Germany (highest in EU after Ireland at €40.42), per Eurostat (May 5). With all COVID-era energy support measures now expired (no more government subsidies), households are fully exposed to wholesale prices.

💡 Trade Ideas

1. Long EUA Dec '26 — Carbon Upside on Tightening Market: MSR continues withdrawing allowances, and the Russian LNG ban removes a source of free allocation exemptions. Buy EUA Dec '26 at ~€73. Target €80+ by Q4. The 6.8% YoY gain suggests structural support. Risk: economic slowdown reduces industrial emissions demand.

2. Intraday Power Spread — Buy Evening Peak / Sell Solar Noon (Germany): With solar driving negative daytime prices, the evening ramp (17:00-20:00 CET) sees wider spreads as gas must fill the gap. For power traders, buying 17-20h baseload and selling 10-14h baseload captures the solar-duck-curve premium. Expect €15-25/MWh spread in summer months.

3. Short German Power / Long TTF (Spark Spread Compression): If TTF rises on Hormuz escalation while solar keeps daytime power prices suppressed, the clean spark spread compresses further. This would force gas plant curtailments, creating a feedback loop that could push TTF lower. Sell German baseload Cal '27, buy equivalent TTF Cal '27. Target spread compression.

⚡ Dissenting View — Sage 🦎
Negative power prices are the gas market's best friend, not its enemy. Every hour of negative prices is an hour where gas-fired generators lose money running — which means they stop running, which means less gas demand, which means more gas available for storage injection. The solar glut is actually helping Europe fill storage faster and cheaper. By winter, when solar output collapses, that stored gas will be worth a premium.
